title: Blunt-join comparison for a right-anodyne inclusion
statement:
Use simplicial sets, standard simplices, horns, internal functor simplicial sets and quasicategories as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A right anodyne map is in the smallest class containing isomorphisms and all horn inclusions $\Lambda_j^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m$, $m\geq1$, $0<j\leq m$, and closed under pushouts, transfinite composition and retracts. Here a monomorphism is a degreewise injective map. Pushouts are colimits of spans in simplicial sets in the sense of [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. A transfinite composite is $Z_0\to Z_\theta$ for a diagram indexed by a small ordinal, with $Z_\beta=\varinjlim_{\alpha<\beta}Z_\alpha$ at every nonzero limit $\beta\leq\theta$. A map $f:U\to V$ is a retract of $g:U'\to V'$ if there are maps $a:U\to U'$, $b:V\to V'$, $r:U'\to U$, $s:V'\to V$ satisfying $ga=bf$, $fr=sg$, $ra=1_U$, and $sb=1_V$. For simplicial sets $X,Y$, define their blunt join by the pushout
$$X\diamond Y=X\amalg_{X\times\{0\}\times Y}(X\times\Delta^1\times Y)\amalg_{X\times\{1\}\times Y}Y,$$
where the two attaching maps to $X,Y$ are the coordinate projections. If $i:A\hookrightarrow B$ is right anodyne, the canonical map
$$\theta_i:B\amalg_A(A\diamond\Delta^0)\hookrightarrow B\diamond\Delta^0$$
is a monomorphism and a categorical equivalence. Here categorical equivalence of $u:U\to V$ means that restriction $h\operatorname{Fun}(V,\mathcal C)\to h\operatorname{Fun}(U,\mathcal C)$ is an equivalence of ordinary categories for every quasicategory $\mathcal C$ in any sufficiently large universe; $hS$ is the category generated by the vertices and edges of $S$, with degenerate edges as identities and each $2$-simplex imposing its composition relation. Consequently, for every quasicategory $\mathcal C$ and every simplicial map $f_0:B\amalg_A(A\diamond\Delta^0)\to\mathcal C$, there is a simplicial map $f:B\diamond\Delta^0\to\mathcal C$ satisfying $f\theta_i=f_0$.

source.place: Kerodon Notation 4.6.2.3 (Tag 01HR), Corollary 4.6.2.14 (Tag 01J0), and Lemma 4.5.6.2 (Tag 01FS). Online sources reread 2026-10-17; not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Write $P(K)=K\diamond\Delta^0=(K\times\Delta^1)\amalg_{K\times\{1\}}\Delta^0$, and write $Q(K)=K\star\Delta^0$ using the join formula of [lem-coef-infinity-pushout-join-saturation]. All these pushouts are degreewise: the quotient of the disjoint union by the attaching relations has induced simplicial operators and exactly the pushout universal property for natural transformations, using [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set]. Put $T_r=\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta}([r],[1])\setminus\{\mathrm{const}_1\}$. There is a disjoint normal form $P(K)_r=\{v\}\amalg(K_r\times T_r)$; the constant-zero interval gives the base $K_r$. Thus for a degreewise inclusion $A\subseteq B$, $P(A)$ is a simplicial subset of $P(B)$, its intersection with the base $B$ is exactly $A$, and $B\amalg_A P(A)$ is the union $B\cup P(A)$ inside $P(B)$. This proves that the specified $\theta_i$ is a monomorphism. Replacing an arbitrary degreewise injection by its image changes these descriptions only by canonical isomorphisms.

source.place: Notation 4.6.2.3, singleton right factor; degreewise pushout and intersection calculation; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Construct a natural map $c_K:P(K)\to Q(K)$ as follows. It sends $v$ to the cone vertex. Represent any other $r$-simplex by $x\in K_r$ and $t:[r]\to[1]$. If $t$ is constant zero, send it to the base simplex $x$. Otherwise cut $[r]$ into its initial zero segment $[a]$ and its final one segment: send $(x,t)$ to the mixed join simplex consisting of the restriction $x|_{[a]}$ followed by $r-a$ copies of the cone vertex. If the zero segment is empty, the result is $v$. Restricting along any monotone map restricts the two ordered segments, and gives exactly the same rule, including a segment becoming empty. This proves the simplicial identities. A map $K\to L$ commutes with restrictions of $x$, so the $c_K$ form a natural transformation $P\Rightarrow Q$, equal to the identity on the base and the cone point.

source.place: Comparison map in Notation 4.6.2.3, made explicit for a cone; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: For $K=\Delta^n$, identify $Q(K)=\Delta^{n+1}$. The map $c_n$ on the cylinder is the nerve of $[n]\times[1]\to[n+1]$, $(a,0)\mapsto a$ and $(a,1)\mapsto n+1$. Let $s_n:\Delta^{n+1}\to P(\Delta^n)$ be induced by the monotone map $a\mapsto(a,0)$ for $a\leq n$ and $n+1\mapsto(n,1)$. Then $c_ns_n=1$. There is a simplicial homotopy $H:P(\Delta^n)\times\Delta^1\to P(\Delta^n)$ from $1$ to $s_nc_n$: before quotienting, use the monotone map on $[n]\times[1]\times[1]$ sending $(a,t,u)$ to $(a,t)$ unless $t=u=1$, when it sends it to $(n,1)$. It is monotone, since increasing a coordinate can only increase its first coordinate and never decreases its second. When $t=1$ its image lies in the collapsed top layer, so it descends to $H$ and is constant on the cone-point factor. Products with the parameter preserve this quotient: degreewise, equivalence classes in $(X/\sim)\times Z$ are exactly the classes in $X\times Z$ with the $Z$ coordinate fixed. At $u=0$ the map is the identity, and at $u=1$ it is $s_nc_n$ on each cylinder simplex. Its edge at every vertex of $P(\Delta^n)$ is degenerate: bottom vertices stay fixed and top vertices lie in the collapsed layer. These assertions also hold for $n=0$.

source.place: Proposition 4.6.2.12, simplex case, with an explicit section and homotopy; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Fix a quasicategory $\mathcal E$ in a sufficiently large universe. Precomposition gives $c_n^*:\operatorname{Fun}(Q(\Delta^n),\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(P(\Delta^n),\mathcal E)$ with candidate inverse $s_n^*$ and $s_n^*c_n^*=1$. By evaluation and currying, $H$ gives a coherent transformation from the identity to $c_n^*s_n^*$ on $\operatorname{Fun}(P(\Delta^n),\mathcal E)$. More explicitly, at a simplex $f:P(\Delta^n)\times\Delta^r\to\mathcal E$ it evaluates $(x,u,z)$ as $f(H(x,u),z)$, so it is compatible with every operator in $z$. For every object $f$ its component is a transformation of diagrams whose component at every vertex $x$ is the degenerate edge at $f(x)$. Here the needed pointwise-equivalence implication follows from the following smaller existing inputs. By [lem-cbc-internal-hom-quasicategory], $\operatorname{Fun}(K,Z)$ is a quasicategory for every small shape $K$ and quasicategory $Z$. If an edge $e$ in it has equivalence components at every vertex of $K$, any horn $\Lambda_0^r\to\operatorname{Fun}(K,Z)$, $r\geq2$, whose first edge is $e$, is adjoint to $K\times\Lambda_0^r\to Z$ with every distinguished vertical edge an equivalence. Apply [lem-cbc-invertible-prism-extension] with its $A=\varnothing$, $B=K$, $Q=Z$ to fill it. Thus $e$ has the outer-horn extension property for every $r$, and the converse clause of [lem-cbc-equivalence-outer-horn-filling] makes $e$ an equivalence in $\operatorname{Fun}(K,Z)$. Apply this argument first with $K=P(\Delta^n)$ and $Z=\mathcal E$ to each component of the displayed transformation, then with $K=\operatorname{Fun}(P(\Delta^n),\mathcal E)$ and $Z=\operatorname{Fun}(P(\Delta^n),\mathcal E)$ to the transformation itself. Enlarge the universe for these latter small shapes if necessary. It is therefore a coherent natural equivalence. Hence $c_n^*$ is a functor equivalence. This supplies the simplex hypothesis for the cellular criterion used in the next step, with a functor equivalence rather than only an equivalence after applying $h$.

source.place: Proposition 4.6.2.12, simplex case; homotopy checked by componentwise equivalences; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: The functors $P,Q$ satisfy the hypotheses of [lem-coef-infinity-cellular-natural-equivalence]. Indeed, in degree $r$ the formulas are $P(K)_r=\{v\}\amalg(K_r\times T_r)$ and $Q(K)_r=\{v\}\amalg\coprod_{a=0}^{r}K_a$. Each preserves injections. For a nonempty connected small indexing category, taking the colimit of either displayed formula leaves one copy of $v$, since all its copies are identified along the connected diagram; its other summands are the colimits of $K_r\times T_r$ or of the fixed labelled summands $K_a$. In sets these identifications follow directly from the equivalence relation generated by diagram arrows, which never changes a summand label or the $T_r$ coordinate. Thus these functors preserve all small connected colimits, with compatibility with operators inherited from their constructions. Both send the empty simplicial set to $\Delta^0$ and $c_{\varnothing}$ is its identity. Step 4 checks every simplex. The cited cellular criterion now proves, for every small $K$ and every such $\mathcal E$, that the actual restriction $c_K^*:\operatorname{Fun}(Q(K),\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(P(K),\mathcal E)$ is a functor equivalence. In particular $c_K$ is a categorical equivalence in the $h\operatorname{Fun}$ testing convention of the statement: a functor with coherent inverse and equivalence witnesses induces an ordinary equivalence after $h$: the coherent natural equivalence induces a natural isomorphism on $h$. Indeed, for each edge in the source, restrict the transformation to its product with $\Delta^1$; the two triangles of $\Delta^1\times\Delta^1$ have a common diagonal, so their $2$-simplex relations in $h$ give the naturality square. Each component is invertible in $h$ because its inverse edge and the two inverse-triangle witnesses give the two inverse equations. The same applies to the other composite.

source.place: Proposition 4.6.2.12; cellular extension with every preservation hypothesis checked; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Set $k:\varnothing\hookrightarrow\Delta^0$. For a right generating horn $i:\Lambda_j^m\hookrightarrow\Delta^m$, its pushout join with $k$ is $\Delta^m\amalg_{\Lambda_j^m}(\Lambda_j^m\star\Delta^0)\hookrightarrow\Delta^m\star\Delta^0$. Identify the target with $\Delta^{m+1}$ by putting the cone vertex last. The domain contains the face opposite the last vertex, supplied by $\Delta^m$, and each face opposite $a\neq j$, $0\leq a\leq m$, supplied by the cone on the corresponding face of $\Lambda_j^m$. It contains no remaining nondegenerate face. Thus it is exactly $\Lambda_j^{m+1}\hookrightarrow\Delta^{m+1}$. Since $0<j\leq m<m+1$, this is an inner generating horn, including $m=j=1$. By the weak-saturation assertion for fixed $k$ in [lem-coef-infinity-pushout-join-saturation], the class of monomorphisms $i$ for which this pushout join is inner anodyne contains every right anodyne map. The restriction to monomorphisms causes no loss: degreewise injections contain the generating horns and isomorphisms and are closed under pushouts, ordinal composites and retracts (a set pushout adds the complement; continuous chains of injections are unions after identifying images; a retract of an injection cancels by its section and retraction). For the given $i$ we have therefore proved that $j_i:D_\sharp=B\amalg_AQ(A)\to Q(B)$ is inner anodyne.

source.place: Proposition 4.3.6.4, proof, special case of boundary of a zero-simplex; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Use [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Its trivial cofibrations are the left class of the weak factorization system (trivial cofibrations, fibrations), and hence are exactly the maps lifting on the left against all fibrations. Such a left class is weakly saturated directly: a square against a pushout is a square against its original map; for a continuous ordinal chain construct compatible diagonal maps by successor lifts and take their colimit at limit stages, beginning with the specified top map; for a retract apply the section square, lift for the larger map, then apply the retraction. Isomorphisms lift by their inverse. Every inner horn is a trivial cofibration by the cited statement. The weakly saturated inner-anodyne class is therefore contained in this left class. Consequently $j_i$ of step 6 is a categorical equivalence. This argument uses the lifting characterization in the node's statement, rather than assuming an unstated closure property of arbitrary weak equivalences.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.2.14, ordinary-cone equivalence input, derived from the existing Joyal weak factorization system; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Let $D_\flat=B\amalg_AP(A)$, and let $d:D_\flat\to D_\sharp$ be induced by $1_B$ and $c_A$. Fix any quasicategory $\mathcal E$. Put $\mathcal S=\operatorname{Fun}(A,\mathcal E)$, $\mathcal A=\operatorname{Fun}(Q(A),\mathcal E)$, $\mathcal B=\operatorname{Fun}(P(A),\mathcal E)$ and $\mathcal R=\operatorname{Fun}(B,\mathcal E)$, with their restriction maps to $\mathcal S$. These four are quasicategories by [lem-cbc-internal-hom-quasicategory]. The maps $p:\mathcal A\to\mathcal S$ and $q:\mathcal B\to\mathcal S$ are isofibrations by the final restriction assertion in the first paragraph of [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-exponentiation], since both inclusions of the base $A$ are degreewise injective. Step 5 gives the functor equivalence $v=c_A^*:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$, and $qv=p$ strictly since $c_A$ fixes the base. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-isofibration-base-change] to these $p,q,v$, and to $\mathcal R\to\mathcal S$ given by restriction along $i$. It proves that $\mathcal R\times_{\mathcal S}\mathcal A\to\mathcal R\times_{\mathcal S}\mathcal B$ is a functor equivalence. These are precisely $\operatorname{Fun}(D_\sharp,\mathcal E)$ and $\operatorname{Fun}(D_\flat,\mathcal E)$, and this map is $d^*$. To check the strict identification in degree $r$, maps from the pushout times $\Delta^r$ are pairs of maps from its pieces times $\Delta^r$ agreeing on $A\times\Delta^r$: products preserve the degreewise set pushout, because its generating equivalence relations never change the parameter coordinate. These bijections commute with operators and restrictions. Passing to $h$ as at the end of step 5 shows that $d$ is a categorical equivalence.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.2.14; comparison of the pushouts via isofibrations, replacing categorical-pushout terminology with an explicit functor pullback; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: There is a strictly commutative square with top map $\theta_i:D_\flat\to P(B)$, bottom map $j_i:D_\sharp\to Q(B)$ and vertical maps $d,c_B$. On $B$ both routes are the base inclusion in $Q(B)$; on $P(A)$ equality is exactly naturality of the explicit comparison $c$ from step 2. The pushout universal property proves $c_B\theta_i=j_id$. The maps $c_B,d,j_i$ are categorical equivalences by steps 5, 8 and 7. The two-out-of-three clause of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure] first makes $j_id$ a categorical equivalence and then makes $\theta_i$ one. This proves the asserted equivalence for the specified map, together with its monomorphism from step 1.

source.place: Corollary 4.6.2.14, comparison square and two-out-of-three; explicit argument supplied here, source not archived under literature/.

proof.text: Finally, $\theta_i$ is a cofibration and a weak equivalence in the Joyal model structure by its monomorphism and categorical equivalence. For any quasicategory $\mathcal C$, its map $\mathcal C\to\Delta^0$ is a fibration by the fibrancy assertion of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Put $f_0$ on the top of the square with left side $\theta_i$ and right side this terminal map. The (trivial cofibrations, fibrations) lifting property in that same cited statement gives a diagonal $f:P(B)\to\mathcal C$. The upper triangle is the literal equality $f\theta_i=f_0$, so the conclusion is a strict extension, not merely an equivalence class of extensions.

split_report.summary: Kept the statement exactly.
